Senses.Explanation: The records deploy ‘single transmission’ as a lineage slogan joined to direct pointing, the mind-seal, and transmission outside teachings. Literally "single, sole" (單) and "transmit" (傳): "transmit singly," attested 692 times in 211 allowlisted texts. Zhongfeng says Bodhidharma's coming west is "called single transmission and direct pointing" and "at first had no twists and turns" (謂之單傳直指，初無委曲). In another address he gives a direct local definition: "the four holy and six ordinary [classes] are each originally complete; this is called single transmission," then asks, "what is transmitted?" (各各本來具足謂單傳，傳箇甚麼). Frequent compounds are "single transmission and direct pointing" (單傳直指), "single transmission of the mind-seal" (單傳心印), and "single transmission outside the teachings" (教外單傳).
Senses.Note: The records place the term in lineage slogans, questions, and verse. One lamp record pairs, "Bodhidharma came from the west, singly transmitting the mind-seal; the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi did not know one written character" (達磨西來，單傳心印，曹溪六祖，不識一字). A later lineage statement says the flower-holding smile was entrusted as "single transmission outside the teachings" (教外單傳). The four direct-question occurrences and twelve "termed single transmission" formulas belong to this shared lineage wording, not master-specific senses.

Senses.Explanation: Single transmission and direct pointing joins two public lineage claims: the teaching is transmitted singly outside proliferating explanatory branches, and it points directly rather than proceeding through imposed symbolism. The records use the formula to name Bodhidharma's arrival, then test later explanations against it; one rejects interpreting Mazu's cart exchange as body-and-mind symbolism precisely because that would not be direct pointing.

Senses.Explanation: To raise singly is to bring one saying, question, or Chan device forward without auxiliary explanation or divided attention. Chan records use the verb with an expressed object: a single word 'no,' the first phrase, the upward move, the command, this matter, or a hair-blowing sharp sword. They also oppose 'raising alone and handling alone' to 'dragging through water and mud,' and place 'raise directly and singly' beside the transmission outside teachings and not establishing written words. The public-interview shape remains visible when an unnamed monastic asks how Yuanwu Keqin treats people while 'today singly raising the command' and receives a blow. The Chan-specific bend is this productive teaching-seat verb: what is singled out may be a word, phrase, matter, sword, move, or command. Because those nouns are different objects of the same transitive act, they do not require separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: Blood under the skin is the records' bodily image for someone who registers pain and itching, unlike unresponsive earth and wood. It is consequently used by Gulin Qingmao as a qualification for people addressed in the hall: "you people must have blood under the skin" (汝諸人須是皮下有血始得), and "if he has blood under the skin, he will certainly have another livelihood" (他若皮下有血，必定別有生涯). A garden exchange also keeps the literal body image audible: seeing a cook cut melons, Yu'an Zhiji asks the head cook, "which one has blood under the skin?" (那個皮下有血). Zen bends the bodily phrase into a recurrent test for someone who registers a touch or blow, while the records themselves ground that use in pain and itching rather than an imported psychological category.
